title: POC translation & extractor scoping - Epsilon Technologies

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-24
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Clara Nguyen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Epsilon Head of AI), Jonas Weber (Epsilon ML Eng), Li Chen (Epsilon Security)

Summary: kickoff to scope a POC focused on multilingual machine translation plus downstream named-entity and concept extraction for Epsilon's contract intake pipeline. Main constraints: throughput for batch ingestion, low-ish tail latency for interactive corrections, and strict audit/KMS requirements.

[00:00] Clara: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick off, i'm clara from redwood, and with me is diego from our se team. how's the audio on your end?
[00:12] Maya: good here, thanks. we wanted to move quickly — this POC is high priority for our product v2, so appreciate the help.
[00:20] Diego: great, quick agenda: we'll confirm success criteria, talk workload shape, propose a small shortlist of open models across size/quant, and then outline the benchmark plan. also security + timeline. any additions?
[00:30] Jonas: that sounds good. one ask, we do want to test bilingual (en->de) and tri-lingual (en, fr, es) flows. also contracts include legal terms, so we care about extraction recall.
[00:45] Clara: noted. to be explicit, success criteria i've seen in other POCs: latency p95 < 250ms for interactive routes (or a clear fallback), extraction F1 > 0.82 on our annotated set, and throughput of ~150 reqs/min on dedicated pool. are those in the ballpark?
[01:10] Maya: F1 target is reasonable. on latency, we might be okay with a slightly higher p95 if cost is drastically lower. we need to see tradeoffs though.
[01:25] Li: security note — we need VPC connectivity for the private control plane option, KMS for encryption at rest, and audit logs retained 1 year. is that supported?
[01:38] Diego: yep, we support VPC + private deploys. KMS integrations available for AWS and GCP, and audit logs exportable to S3/Cloud Storage. i'll follow up with the SOC2/ISO docs.
[01:50] Jonas: about models — what's the baseline you recommend? we've tried small transformer models but the legal language is noisy.
[02:05] Clara: for extraction-heavy tasks we usually recommend testing a 3-point shortlist: 1) a compact quantized model (e.g., 7B int8) for low-cost fast throughput, 2) a medium-size 13B float/quant hybrid for quality, 3) a larger 70B or LLaMA2-70B variant for highest quality where latency allows. but for multilingual legal, a mid-size often wins due to domain generalization.
[02:40] Maya: curious which open checkpoints you had in mind. we've got licensing constraints, prefer permissive so we can fine-tune/evaluate locally.
[02:50] Diego: understood — our shortlist will focus on permissively licensed Llama-family forks and M2/RedPajama derivatives available under compatible terms. we'll include quantized variants to show cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:05] Clara: i'll also note that redwood has a model variant routing feature — if the medium model fails quality thresholds on a sample, you can fall back to the larger model for that request class. that helps balance cost. (note: transcript sometimes shows product names as 'redwood model route' or 'redwood rout')
[03:30] Jonas: ok. for benchmarking, can you outline metrics you'll collect out of the box? we want token costs, latency distribution, mem usage, and per-class F1.
[03:45] Diego: yes: tokens per request, per-token compute time, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, achieved throughput at target latency, and model quality metrics (F1, exact match). we'll supply the harness and ingest script.
[04:05] Maya: perfect. about dataset — we'll provide 10k anonymized contracts, but only ~1k will be labeled for entity spans. is that enough?
[04:18] Diego: enough for a quick POC. we'll do cross-validation and also synthetic augmentation if you want. initial evals will run on the labeled set; the rest will be used for stress tests.
[04:35] Li: question about data in flight — are token payloads logged in any way on hosted? our compliance policy requires redaction and limited retention.
[04:45] Clara: on hosted, request logs can be suppressed; by default we keep minimal metadata. for highest assurance you'll want private deployment where we can ensure customer-managed storage and optional redact. we'll include that option in the doc.
[05:02] Jonas: ok. can you share estimated cost delta between the 7B int8 and 13B q4 for our workload? rough numbers are fine.
[05:12] Diego: rough back-of-envelope: on dedicated GPUs with batching, 7B int8 can be 3-4x cheaper per token vs 13B q4; 13B yields 10-15% better F1 typically on extraction for domain-ish text, but depends on prompts. we'll quantify during the benchmark run.
[05:40] Maya: timeline wise — we have a product demo in mid April. can the POC be 6 weeks and give us a recommended model + perf numbers by then?
[05:52] Clara: 6 weeks is doable: week 0: kickoff + data exchange, week 1-2: initial benchmark runs on shortlist, week 3: iterate prompts/quant settings, week 4: end-to-end tests and throughput tuning, week 5: security + private deploy validation, week 6: final report and recommended model.
[06:15] Jonas: sounds good, any blockers you see?
[06:20] Diego: only if we don't get the labeled set quickly or if there are licensing blockers for a model. otherwise we can parallelize benchmarking across model variants.
[06:30] Li: regarding private deploys, we need to validate HSM/KMS key rotation policies. can you provide tech contact for that?
[06:38] Clara: yes, i'll put Diego as the technical lead and add our infra security doc.
[06:45] Maya: let's talk about multilingual strategy — we care about en->de translation quality plus entity extraction in target language. do you recommend translating to en then extracting, or extract in target language?
[06:58] Diego: both have tradeoffs. pipeline A: translate->extract tends to simplify extraction because extractor works in canonical English space but may introduce translation errors. Pipeline B: multilingual extractor avoids translation noise but requires a model with strong multilingual understanding. For contracts, we've seen higher recall using a bilingual extractor trained or adapted to target language; for low-resource language or very domain-specific terms, translate->extract with domain fine-tune sometimes wins. we'll include both in the benchmark scenarios.
[07:35] Jonas: okay include both pipelines and compare end-to-end F1 plus latency/cost.
[07:42] Clara: agreed. i'll include pipeline labels in the benchmark template.
[07:48] Maya: do you support token-level caching or prefix KV caching for repeated clauses? some of our contracts have standard boilerplate repeated many times.
[07:58] Diego: yes, redwood runtime supports prefix caching and KV cache reuse for completions; for extraction we can leverage cached encodings for repeated paragraphs to reduce cost. we'll show that in the throughput tests. note: transcript mis-heard as 'prefix K V cat' sometimes.
[08:18] Li: last security Q — do you do penetration testing on on-prem packages?
[08:23] Diego: we provide a report of our internal security posture; for on-prem we can facilitate a joint pentest and share procedures. details in the security pack.
[08:35] Clara: quick check — are there any hard constraints we haven't covered?
[08:40] Maya: SLA negotiable, but we'd like redwood to meet our internal cost targets; also legal needs to review model license before any fine-tune.
[08:52] Clara: understood — we'll include licensing info per checkpoint.
[09:00] Jonas: on instrumentation, how do you expose per-route cost? can we get token-level breakdown for each API call?
[09:10] Diego: yes, console exposes cost by route/model/token breakdown, plus traces you can hook into. we'll give you a demo link.
[09:20] Maya: great. one more — do you have any existing rules-of-thumb for batching config for this throughput?
[09:28] Diego: rule of thumb: for latency-sensitive interactive routes use small batch sizes and aggressive KV caching; for bulk ingestion use larger batch sizes and dedicate GPU pools. we'll test both and propose autoscaling policies.
[09:45] Clara: ok, to recap next steps: we'll send model shortlist + benchmark template, diego will prep perf harness, maya will share sample dataset, and Li will review security docs. schedule perf kickoff next week; i will send calendar invites.
[10:05] Maya: thanks, looking forward.
[10:09] Clara: thanks all.

End notes: rough timestamps above cover the substantive part of the call; following 40 minutes contained deeper technical Q&A and a 15-minute detour about their internal annotation schema which included examples and an off-record discussion around license review. Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions of product names and acronyms.
